To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the grain trade was a key factor in Kent's economic and political development.
the grain market of Kent, England's most populous shire in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, was dominated by merchant oligarchs in its three main ports.

the grain trade in Kent was concentrated in the hands of a merchant oligarchy, and that this oligarchy was able to exploit their market power to the disadvantage of the rural population, and to the advantage of the townsfolk of Kent, and the urban poor of London.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the structure of the grain trade, and its relationship to the development of market relations and regional specialization; the politics of grain trade and the politics of subsistence; the relationship between the politics of dearth and those of plenty; the relationship between popular and elite politics in periods of subsistence crisis; the relationship between local and regional politics.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Kent's grain trade, and the politics of its regulation, were shaped by the interaction of a number of factors.
the politics of dearth in early modern England was shaped by the politics of plenty.
the grain trade of the Kentish ports was the principal cause of the social and political tensions of the period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have sought to understand the structure and politics of the grain trade by placing the grain trade within a broader context of social and economic relations.
we have shown how the grain trade in Kent was structured and developed during the early modern period, and how it was affected by the politics of dearth.
the grain trade in Kent was not only the product of the commercialization of agriculture but a major agent of that process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the politics of dearth were not simply a product of the structural and political tensions that arose from the development of market exchange and agrarian specialization in the early modern economy, but also reflected the politics of plenty.
the politics of dearth was a product of the politics of market integration, and that it was shaped as much by the vertical as by the horizontal fissures of the social structure.
we need to be much more sensitive to the ways in which local elites, in their own self-interested ways, helped shape the politics of the poor in their own localities.
